  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Shouting: Shouting, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Vignette:
Kofi had always been drawn to the precision and control of his work as a bomb disposal technician. He took pride in being able to diffuse even the most complex devices, often finding solace in the methodical nature of his job. But all of that changed on the day a massive earthquake struck his hometown, destroying entire city blocks and leaving thousands homeless. As Kofi navigated the rubble-filled streets, he was struck by the sheer unpredictability of it all. Buildings that had stood for decades were reduced to piles of dust and debris in an instant. The sounds of screams and crumbling concrete still echoed in his mind, and the memory of the earth shaking beneath his feet made him feel like he was walking on shaky ground even now. In the months that followed, Kofi found himself becoming increasingly withdrawn. He would avoid social gatherings or any situation that might be stressful, citing work commitments or fatigue as excuses. His wife, Ama, noticed the change in him and tried to get him to open up, but Kofi just couldn't shake off the feeling of being on edge all the time. He started eating more, using food as a way to calm his nerves. A few extra pounds didn't seem like such a big deal when it meant he could avoid thinking about the earthquake for a little while longer. And so, the weight crept on, along with the avoidance behaviors that had become second nature to him. But even with all the distractions, Kofi's body still reacted as if it was waiting for the other shoe to drop. Loud noises would send his heart racing, and he'd find himself scanning the room for potential threats before he even realized what was happening. It got to the point where Ama would have to remind him that there was no danger, that they were safe. The memories of that day still lingered, but Kofi found it hard to recall them fully. He'd get flashes of images – a building collapsing, people running for cover – but they'd be disjointed and incomplete. And when he did manage to piece together some of the events, rage would well up inside him. Why had this happened? Why couldn't anyone have predicted it? Kofi's work began to suffer as a result. He'd get false alarms during disposal procedures, his body reacting before his mind could process what was happening. His colleagues started to notice, and soon he was being passed over for jobs that required the kind of focus and calm he used to possess. It wasn't until Ama sat him down one evening, her eyes filled with tears, that Kofi realized he needed help. She told him she couldn't keep watching him like this – distant, on edge, and slowly unraveling. The earthquake may have shaken their city, but it was Kofi's own internal tremors that were now threatening to destroy their life together. As Kofi sat in his therapist's office for the first time, he knew he had a long road ahead of him. He wasn't sure what the future held or how he'd learn to manage these feelings of perpetual threat, but he was willing to try. For Ama, for himself, and for the life they once knew – he was ready to face whatever lay ahead, even if it meant confronting the very memories he'd been trying so hard to avoid.
